item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
This tale blew me away. The nuance and depth with which it touches on issues of autonomy/agency, othering, the all-too-often binary nature of the judgments of mass culture, and the entire oxymoron of "corporate ethics"—how it produces these structural inhumanities and then sits judge and jury over everyone swept into them—and more than anything else, that it's fundamentally a character drama, and never has to step outside of itself to raise these questions directly in a heavy-handed, unnatural way. It also does such an excellent job of setting up what I imagine a post-Veil world would really feel like, which I guess is to say not at all very different from our own—the cultural and ethical problematics wouldn't really be fundamentally too different, and this tale captures that so well.

I didn't mean to gush, but like this is now my favorite piece in a canon full of excellent writing. pls take all my +1

Thanks for responding!

I just reread this tale, and I still can't help but like the couple, even though I get what you're saying. I think the reason I like the pairing so much is because SCP-4427-B is eerily similar to a special person for me, right down to the trans, the BDSM, and manipulative tendencies. And despite that, I feel my experience with them was overwhelmingly positive. Maybe I'm just viewing it all with rose-tinted glasses, it's hard not to see the similarities, to read in mine own desires in it. I often catch myself wishing that things could've worked out, that our respective instabilities and mental issues wouldn't have precluded it, as they ultimately did. And… I wish she were still alive.

Sorry, that got dark. But, yeah, I don't mean to fetishize the incredible power imbalance inherent to Reggie's and Jasper's relationship, or their manipulative tendencies or mental instability, it's just… hard not to see the similarities. And wish for things that cannot be.

item.content:encoded:
I'm glad you liked it!

I'm just dying to hear what happens to them afterwards. Do they ever get reunited? Things like that.

spoilers I guess
_

They're definitely not. Not in this reality construct, at least. Even if Jacobson gets off the hook somehow (the Ethics Committee will make sure he doesn't), the anomaly is still not going anywhere and will be kept very separate from Jacobson, though it's unlikely he'll even be in the same facility at all.

I don't want to intrude on you liking them as a couple, because when I write relationships I'm always interested in seeing how they're viewed, but to me this is the happy ending; 4427 has some manipulative personality tendencies and is kind of an unstable asshole in general whether intentional or not (see here), and Jacobson wasn't interested in sexually engaging with them at all until they made multiple advances on him and he eventually felt pressured into it. Their whole relationship is not organic or natural, it's twisted and distorted by the presence of the Foundation and the roles thus forced upon the individuals in question.

The only question I have left: Was there more to their relationship than just recreational sex? Like, were they actually in love with each other, and could they admit it?

I don't think either of them is in a healthy enough psychological place to know.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
As someone that's into occasionally risky or extreme play, I also tend to favor RACK. But that doesn't mean I'd abuse my power to have sexual play with someone I had IRL power over. The issue isn't the A- aware- it's the C, consent- a prisoner can't give consent to sleep with his jailer, because he isn't free. If he chooses to withdraw consent, well, then dangerous things can happen if his partner isn't a decent person. Which is why stuff like this can't happen; there's a difference between risky play and a toxic, morally questionable relationship.

Eh, but I'm getting passionate about ethical quandaries in a piece of fiction. Ha, that there is a testament to your writing skills.

EDIT: I want to revise the above statement, because I don't feel like I expressed my position very well, and honestly the implications of this tale have been jangling around in my head. I think that in a situation where one party has the explicit ability to make life worst for the other, consent, whether aware and informed or not, is necessarily diminished. Even if you engage in the relationship willingly, a boss sleeping with an employee, a doctor sleeping with a patient, or a prison guard sleeping with an inmate must be treated as non-consensual, because the other, vulnerable party's ability or inclination to withdraw consent would be compromised.

Damned thought-provoking piece. Kudos

item.content:encoded:
As someone involved in the BDSM community, who spends a lot of time thinking about sexual ethics and the importance of informed consent, this really spoke to me.

Props to you for speaking openly about your involvement in the community; that was a big influence for me too when writing this, though for some reason even I felt weird mentioning it in the author post. But it's there and it's significant.

+ show block
– hide block

Edit: Relatedly, I forgot to mention that my thought process while writing the two main viewpoints of the central ethical argument was to compare them to SSC and RACK, with the Ethics Committee arguing that their activities would need to be Safe, Sane, and Consensual to be ethical, and the SCP's argument being that their activities need only meet the parameters of Risk-Aware Consensual Kink to be ethical. The anomaly states that because they are aware of their situation and the factors that make it unethical in the eyes of the Foundation, they are able to consent and thus it's not the Committee's business what they want. The Committee believes that even if activities are private and consensual — in the "short-term, surface-level meaning of the word", as they said — they violate society's ethical standards and that overrides those of the individual even when done in private.

As a RACK person I knew that I could end up writing biased toward the anomaly's side, which is why I took great focus on showcasing the logic of the Ethic's Committee's stance contrasted with the deeply personal emotion of the anomaly's stance. Hopefully that worked, and it seems like it did, because I started writing this with the intention of the reader taking the side of the couple and not the side of bureaucracy. But it seems I made it disturbingly balanced, even in how I as the author see it, which is a result I like more.

Edit: I'm gonna leave the above the way I originally wrote it for the sake of the comments record, but it ought to be stated somewhere that I fully agree with the response below. The issue I was trying to illustrate would be that 4427-B doesn't, and their argument is that denying them the right to have that perspective is contradictory to the argument that they should be treated with respect and as a sapient entity. (And the example of being in jail is nonconsensual in and of itself; their containment situation is not.) I don't agree with them, but I know and knew people who would, and they're not what one would call bad people. That's what's tricky about it; that's what's gross about it, even.
